turns.t: Mr Chaudhry? Mr Rashid Chaudhry, is that right?
Yes, that is correct. Good morning, Doctor, and thank you for seeing me.
My pleasure. And who has come along with you?
I'm Nadia, his daughter. I take him to dialysis most weeks, so I see what goes on at home.
That's very helpful to have. So, Mr Chaudhry, the unit tells me you've been struggling with the fluid limit. Tell me about it in your own words.
Yes. I confess I find it very difficult. I am thirsty almost all of the time, and I try to be disciplined, but it is a real struggle.
Thirsty almost all of the time. That sounds exhausting. When is it at its worst?
The long gap over the weekend. By Sunday evening I could drink the tap dry.
He keeps a glass by his chair, Doctor, and it ends up empty. Then his ankles blow up by Monday morning.
Ankles swelling by Monday. Is that how it seems to you, Mr Chaudhry?
Quite so. They are rather swollen on Mondays, and my shoes become a trial.
Swollen ankles at the end of the long gap. Is there anything else, during the dialysis itself?
Cramps, occasionally. In the calves, towards the last hour. They are quite painful, though they pass.
Cramps in the last hour of the session, thank you. Let me ask about a few other things. Any chest pain?
No, none.
Any trouble breathing when you lie flat at night?
No, I sleep perfectly well flat, with one pillow.
And any itching of the skin?
No, not at present.
That's all good news. Now your background. How long have the kidneys been failing?
Kidney failure for six years now. I was told it came from the high blood pressure, which I have had for twenty years. I also have gout, which flares up now and then.
And the access for your dialysis, how was that arranged?
I had a fistula put in my arm, four years ago. It works very well.
Good. And what tablets are you taking at the moment?
Sevelamer, 800 milligrams with meals, for the phosphate. Amlodipine, 5 milligrams once a day. And folic acid, 5 milligrams in the morning.
I fill his pill box on Sundays, so I know where everything stands.
Lovely, Nadia. So that's sevelamer with meals, amlodipine once a day, and folic acid in the morning. Are you allergic to anything, Mr Chaudhry? Any allergies at all?
No, I have no allergies, Doctor.
Dad, what about that antibiotic last year, in the hospital? You had a bad reaction to it. I don't remember which one it was.
I do not recall any such thing. I think you may be mistaken, Nadia.
Maybe. But the nurse did stop it, I remember that much.
Let's keep both in mind for now. Mr Chaudhry recalls no allergies, Nadia remembers a reaction to an antibiotic, and we won't settle it today.
Very well.
Now let me have a look at your ankles, if I may.
By all means.
There's definite puffiness at the ankles, and it dents when I press with my thumb.
Is that serious?

It's what we'd expect when fluid builds up over the long weekend gap. I can't rule out that your target weight on dialysis needs adjusting too, so we'll keep that in mind. Let me say it back: the thirst drives the drinking, the drinking builds the fluid, and the fluid shows in your ankles and your cramps.
That makes sense.

A few practical things. Use a small cup, not a glass. Suck on ice chips or a sugar-free sweet when the thirst bites. Go easy on salt, because salt makes you thirstier. And spread your allowance through the day.
He does love his pickles, Doctor.
Nadia, please.
Pickles are salt in disguise, Mr Chaudhry, so perhaps weekends only for now. So: small cup, ice chips, less salt, spread it out.
I shall certainly try.
If the swelling isn't better by next week, come and see me again. And do tell the dialysis nurses about the cramps, they can often adjust things during the session.
Thank you, Doctor. You have been most kind.
You're very welcome. Look after him, Nadia.
I will. Thank you.
